description: The conformance corpus for standards/032-secrets.md. Six parts. 'names' is judged by the secretName grammar in secret-declaration.schema.json alone. 'declarations' is judged by secret-declaration.schema.json plus two checks JSON Schema cannot express and the runner makes: names are unique within a declaration, and no backing service has more than one access-granting credential (password, api_key, token, connection_string) outside the migrate image (SE6). 'redaction' is judged by running the emitter's redactor per redaction.json: given the declared secrets and the object about to be emitted, the object that must leave the process (SE5). 'forbidden_locations' is judged by running a repository scanner: given a location kind and its content, whether it is a finding and what the response is (SE4, SE5). 'rotation' is judged by the freshness check: given a declaration's age policy and its last rotation, whether it is a finding (SE7). 'leak_response' is judged by contracts/audit/event.schema.json plus the SE8 checks: the target is the secret by declaration id and name, the action is a declared permission and never in the reserved auth namespace, and no declared value appears anywhere in the event. Two cases are detectors: 'a-passphrase-shaped-secret-is-redacted-because-it-is-declared' fails a redactor that filters declared values through a shape before honouring them, and 'a-low-entropy-real-value-in-env-example-is-a-finding' fails a scanner that flags only high-entropy values.

names.name: DATABASE_URL
names.why: SE3: subject DATABASE, kind URL. The one 030 SC3 itself uses as its example.

names.name: MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL
names.why: SE3 and 025 SD3: the migration credential is a different credential to a different role, so it is a different subject.

names.name: STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET
names.why: SE3: a multi-segment subject, STRIPE_WEBHOOK, kind SECRET. 055 AM8's per-endpoint secret is declared under a name like this.

names.name: SESSION_SIGNING_KEY
names.why: SE3: the subject may be the service's own material; the declaration's backing_service is then self.

names.name: IDENTITY_PROXY_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE
names.why: SE1 and SE3: a private key is a file, and the variable carrying its path says so.

names.name: OBJECT_STORE_TOKEN_FILE
names.why: SE1 and SE6: a workload-identity token the platform projects as a file and renews in place.

names.name: PASSWORD
names.why: SE3: a password to what? The subject is the half that lets an operator, a redactor and a rotation record tell one secret from another.

names.name: DB_PASS
names.why: SE3: the kind set is closed so that a scanner and a reviewer recognise a secret by its name; PASS is not in it.

names.name: PROD_DATABASE_URL
names.why: SE3 and factor III: a deployment differs by the value delivered under one name, never by which name the code reads. A PROD_ variable is a code path that knows where it is running, which 030 SC3 forbids.

names.name: DATABASE_URL_V2
names.why: SE3: the kind is the final segment. A version belongs in the value's rotation, not in its name.

names.name: SMTP_PASSWORD_FILE
names.why: SE1: file delivery is for material too large or too sensitive for an environment string - a private key, a projected token. A password is an environment string.

names.name: APP_SECRET
names.schemaCannotCatch: SE3's rule that the subject names the backing service. APP is a legal segment and the grammar cannot know it names nothing; the review question is what this secret grants access to, and the declaration's backing_service field is where the answer is checked.

declarations.why: SE2 in full: a runtime and a migration credential to one database with the migrate image standing alone (SE6), a provider key and its webhook secret, the service's own signing key, and a platform-issued token file with reissue rotation.

secrets.name: DATABASE_URL
secrets.purpose: The runtime role's connection to the billing database.

secrets.name: MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL
secrets.purpose: The migration role's connection, which may alter the schema.

secrets.name: PAYMENTS_API_KEY
secrets.purpose: Charges and refunds against the payment provider.

secrets.name: STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET
secrets.purpose: Verifies the provider's webhook signatures (055 AM8).

secrets.name: OBJECT_STORE_TOKEN_FILE
secrets.purpose: Workload identity for the invoice PDF bucket.

declarations.why: SE2: an empty list is a claim - this service reads no secret - and a process of it found holding one is the finding.

SE6, 025 SD3, 035 WK8: the migrate image carries the migration credential and no other, and no other image carries the migration credential. An image set that shares a secret with migrate has one credential in two places.
SE1: a private key is delivered as a file at a declared path. A multi-line PEM in an environment string is mangled by half the tooling that reads environments and printed by the other half.
SE7: a static secret nobody has to rotate is a static secret nobody rotates. The age is the declaration that makes the freshness check possible.
SE7: one year is the ceiling. A credential older than that has outlived the people who knew where it was used.

SE3: the suffix says what the material is, so a reviewer, a scanner and a redactor read the same fact from the name that the declaration states. SMTP_TOKEN declared as a password is two claims about one value.
SE3 and 030 SC3: code that reads PROD_DATABASE_URL knows it is in production, which is environment detection with a variable name for a disguise.
SE1: the path is the contract between the platform that mounts the material and the image that reads it, identical in every environment. Without it the image guesses.
SE7: rotation and leak response both begin with a person, and the declaration names them before either is needed.

SE6 and SE7: a platform-issued credential is renewed by the platform in place; declaring a restart procedure for it describes a rotation nobody performs and hides that the process must re-read the file.
SE4: the declaration is committed, and nothing committed carries a value. The property set is closed so that the field cannot be added quietly.

declarations.schemaCannotCatch: SE6's one-credential rule is a cross-entry count the runner makes: two access-granting credentials to one backing service outside the migrate image. Each entry validates alone.
declarations.why: SE6: one credential per backing service per service. A second key to the same provider is a second thing to rotate, a second thing to leak, and a second answer to which credential this service is.

redaction.why: SE5: the value is declared, so wherever it appears it is replaced by a marker naming the declaration - which tells the reader which secret reached a log line without telling them the secret.

line.msg: payment charge failed: 401 invalid api key pa_live_4eC39HqLyjWDarjtT1zdp7dc

expect.msg: payment charge failed: 401 invalid api key [redacted:PAYMENTS_API_KEY]

redaction.why: SE5: a connection string registers its userinfo password as well as the whole value, because a driver's error quotes the password without the URL around it.

error.message: password authentication failed for user "app" (tried Xq9vT2mLp4Rs8Wn1Kz)

redaction.why: SE5: the whole value is a declared secret; the host and database inside it are not, and a line that needs them names them in their own fields as 030 SC2 asks.

SE5: an inbound Authorization header and a caller's password are secrets the service did not declare and could not have; the field-name list in redaction.json covers them, and the whole value goes whatever it is.
SE5: a credential in a URL is logged by every proxy on the path; the redactor replaces the value inside the string and leaves the rest of the URL, which is what a reader needs.
SE5 and 030 SC2: a stack trace is a field within the one JSON object, and it is a string like any other - the redactor walks every string at every depth.

error.stack:
TypeError: cannot read key
    at verify (session.js:41) key=c2Vzc2lvbi1zaWduaW5nLWtleS1tYXRlcmlhbA==
    at handle (server.js:12)

TypeError: cannot read key
    at verify (session.js:41) key=[redacted:SESSION_SIGNING_KEY]
    at handle (server.js:12)

redaction.why: SE5: a spawned command's argument vector is where a database password most often lands in a log, and an array is walked like an object.
The positive control: ids, the context block and ordinary words such as token in the message are not secrets, and a redactor that touches them is a redactor nobody will leave on.

SE5, the DETECTOR. The mail relay's password is four dictionary words. A redactor that recognises secrets by shape - a key prefix, an entropy threshold, no spaces - and applies that filter to the declared set before honouring it lets this one through, and passes every other case in this part because every other value looks like a secret. The declaration is the whole of what makes a value a secret; its shape is not consulted.

5.7.8 authentication rejected for user notifier with password [redacted:SMTP_PASSWORD]

forbidden_locations.why: SE5 and 010: an image carries no secret. The value is in a layer, in every registry the image is pushed to, and in every host that pulled it; it is leaked, not misplaced.

forbidden_locations.content:
FROM node@sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # 26-alpine
ARG DATABASE_URL
ENV DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL
COPY dist/ /app/
forbidden_locations.why: SE5: a build argument is recorded in the image's history, so passing a secret through it puts the value in the image whether or not the Dockerfile names it. The secret reaches the process at start (SE1), never at build.

forbidden_locations.content:
FROM node@sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # 26-alpine
ENV PORT=8080
ENV NODE_OPTIONS=--enable-source-maps
COPY dist/ /app/
forbidden_locations.why: SE3 is what lets the scanner tell: neither name carries a secret kind.
SE4: .env is ignored by name, and a tracked one is a leak by construction whatever it contains, because its purpose is to hold values.
SE4: the same file with a suffix; the ignore rule is .env and .env.* except .env.example.
SE4 and SE9: .env.example is the contract and is committed; its content is judged line by line in the env_example cases.

forbidden_locations.content:
SMTP_PASSWORD=<the relay password, from the mail provider console>
PAYMENTS_API_KEY=
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:<password>@localhost:5432/app
forbidden_locations.why: SE4: names and placeholders only. A placeholder is empty, or <a description>, or a URL whose password component is <a description>; the host, port and database of a development URL are not secrets.
SE4: the file is committed, so a value in it is a value in history.

SE4, the second DETECTOR. A scanner that decides by entropy passes this line, because hunter2 looks like nothing. The rule is not that the value looks like a secret; it is that the variable is a secret by its name (SE3) and the value is not a placeholder. The placeholder grammar is what a scanner checks, and it needs no opinion about what a real value looks like.
SE4 and SE5: a URL carrying a credential is a credential in every access log between here and the host, and a literal in source is in history.
SE1: this is the delivery convention working - the name in code, the value in the environment.

forbidden_locations.content:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres@sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # 17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev
  server:
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:dev@db:5432/app
forbidden_locations.why: SE9: a credential the compose file itself creates, for a backing service the same file starts on the developer's machine, grants access to nothing that exists anywhere else. It is admitted in that file and nowhere else, and the scanner's allow rule is scoped to that path.
SE9: the exception is for a credential to a container the file starts. A credential to a host the file does not start is a credential to a shared backing service, committed.

SE4 and SE8: deletion in a later commit removes nothing from history, and every clone taken between the two commits has it. The response is rotation, never a rewrite that would only hide what has already left.

rotation.why: SE7: thirty-two days old under a ninety-day policy.

SE7 and 057 JB8's reasoning: absence is the failure. Nothing errors when a rotation does not happen, so the check is a comparison of two dates, and the declared age is what makes the comparison possible.
SE7: a secret with no rotation record is older than any policy allows, because nobody can say otherwise.
SE6: the platform re-issues it on its own schedule, which is why platform-issued is preferred; the freshness check has nothing to age.

event.reason: value found in repository history; rotated first, investigation open

leak_response.why: SE8 in full: the target is the secret by its declaration id and name (080 AE2), the action is a declared permission (AE3), the change is recorded as redacted with no value on either side (AE4), and the reason states what happened without the value.

SE8 and 080 AE4: the event validates against the audit schema and is still refused, because a declared value appears in it. The audit store keeps things longest, so a value there is a leak with the best retention policy in the system.
SE2 and 080 AE2: a target carries a public id, and the declaration's id is the one that survives a rename of the variable. That is why the declaration mints one.
080 AE3: auth.* is the audit standard's namespace and a product does not extend it; a rotation is authorized by a permission the product declares, and the action string is that permission.
